checks.explanation:
The tree's KO+2 says Black lives with s=0, o=1. It does not. White uses its one threat to retake at A18. Black must connect at B17, because White B17 would capture A17, A16 and B16. White then throws in at A19 instead of playing the slack E19, and Black takes the four stones with C18. White B19 is the only move that keeps a ko; every other White move there lets Black live. Black's only try is A19, since A18 or C19 leave one two-point eye. White A18 then captures, so the new corner ko is White-first, and Black, with no threats, dies. When the threats are equal, Black wins. At (1,1), Black retakes at once and is back at the leaf with (0,0), which is alive. Or it uses its threat in the second ko. So the leaf is KO+, and KO+2 only comes from White's E19 line.

The narrow-area counted tables match this at every step, all at s=0, o=0:
- After A18!, every Black move dies.
- After B17, only W A19 kills.
- After C18, only W B19 kills.
- After B19, every Black move dies, A19 included.

I looked for holes and found none:
- The bottom resource (Black B14, then A14 or C15 against A15/B15) needs a preparatory move that is not itself a threat. Black's only free tempo is right after the A19 throw-in, and White spends its own free tempo answering at C15. In the second ko, B14 is no threat, so White simply connects at A19 and the later atari comes too late.
- In the second ko, Black C19 and E19 are self-atari.
- Black cannot gain liberties along the top edge.
- The wider area's '?' is a solver limitation, not a Black resource. It stays undecided even on clearly dead positions, for example after B14 A19 C19 A19 at a 2M budget.

The tree's S[KO+2] is wrong and the right label is plain KO+. Black's A19 just captured the ko, so Black took first, and White needs a threat to retake. KO+2 claims White needs one more threat than that. In besogo, KO+2 means "White needs 1 threat to start the ko" (extraThreats=1, so Black wins when s >= o-1). The site's tutorial calls it a two-step ko that "becomes KO+ if the opponent won it once". That reading is not a convention the author follows: in this same tree, a capture by the side that just moved is "took first" (leaf ...C18 B17 is KO-). Decisive line: A18! (White's threat) B17 (forced, or White B17 takes three stones) A19 (throw-in, giving up four stones) C18 B19 A19 A18. White takes the new corner ko first, so with s=0, o=1 Black dies. With s=0, o=0, Black C18 captures two stones and lives. With s=1, o=1, Black retakes A19 and C19 lives. So Black wins exactly when s >= o: KO+, with no number and no approach moves. KO+2 needs White to play the slack E19 after B17, which lets Black retake for free. There is no double ko and no ten-thousand-year ko. The bent-four shape becomes a ko at once, and even counting it as dead would still give KO+. Black's local resource (B14 then A14 against A15-B15) is what makes sibling leaf 8 KO+. Here it needs a preparation move that Black never gets: B17, C18 and A19 are all forced, and B14 instead of C18 loses to E19. Solver checks (scratch .../9-c000-definitions/, medium3.py): the plain wider area stays undecided even at a 2M budget, so I added only the bottom points with D15 filled, which takes away Black's C15 cut. In that model, the leaf at (0,0) and (1,1) are Black wins, and (0,1) fails. The (0,1) result was put together from decided sub-positions: every Black reply to A18! fails, the throw-in position fails, every Black reply to B19 fails, and at the second ko B14, A14 or pass followed by White A19 is DEAD. With D15 open, the C15 cut gives Black at most a second atari after a preparation move, and Black has no free move for that.

checks.explanation:
I could not refute the analyst. At the leaf Black has to retake B16 straight away, using a threat. Every other move (A18, B19, C19, E19, a lower-side move or pass) lets White connect at B16 and Black is dead. A18 leaves only the B19-C19 two-point eye. After C19 or B19, A17 is still in atari, so the A18 eye is a ko only White can start and Black can never settle.

After B16!, White's only winning move is B19, an atari on A19. It is a free local threat:
- Black C19 captures, but the ban has lapsed and White retakes at B17. Black needs a second threat.
- Black B17 connects and White A18 captures A19. If Black cannot retake, White sacrifices three stones at A19. Black captures at C19 and White plays the vital point A19 of the bent three. The solver says DEAD here even with s=3.
- Black A18 leaves only one eye, at B19.

Search-area counts give Black alive exactly when s >= o+2: (1,0) no, (2,0) yes, (2,1) no, (3,1) yes, (3,2) no, (4,2) yes. The s=2 line is B16! B19 C19 B17 B16!: White has no local move left and Black connects at B17, living with eyes at A18 and B19.

In the wider area (1,0) is undecided, but that is a solver limit. It cannot even prove the plainly dead bent-three position, and decides it as dead once the lower side is settled with C15.

Reading the lower side: White's A16/A15/B15 group has three liberties. Black needs a preparatory move, B14 or C15, before A14 becomes a threat, and White can always answer A14 by connecting at C15. Each time Black spends that move, White uses the tempo to end the fight: connect at B16, retake at B17, or the A19 sacrifice. So it never becomes a working threat. Black has no other local threat on the top edge or elsewhere.

The author probably missed the B19 atari, or took the corner ko after B17/A18 for the KO+ shape of the sibling leaf. That sibling has a bent four after the sacrifice; here it is a bent three. The tree's KO- (Black wins when s >= o+1) is wrong, and the right label is KO-2.

At the leaf White has just captured at B17 (direct ko, White took first, no approach move), so the baseline is KO-, but White also owns a free local threat. After Black retakes B16! (using a threat), W B19 (atari on A19) forces either B C19 (capture), after which White retakes B17 without a threat, or B B17 (connect), after which W A18 captures A19 and starts a new direct corner ko that White has taken (if White wins it: W A19 connect, B C19 takes three stones, W A19 vital point = dead bent three). Either way Black needs a second threat, so Black wins iff s >= o+2, which is besogo's KO-2 ('Black needs 1 threat to start the ko'). Counted search in the search area: (1,0) dies, (2,0) lives, (2,1) dies, (3,1) lives, (3,2) dies, (4,2) lives. After B16! at (0,0), W B19 is White's only killing move; after B16! B19 Black needs one more threat whether it plays C19 or B17 (A18, E19 and pass fail even with one). Wider area: the only real extra resource is Black against A16/A15/B15 (B14/A14/C15), which needs two moves before it is even an atari and is answered at C15. In a medium area (search area plus A14 B14 C15 D15 A13 B13) I proved the corner ko after B16! B19 B17 A18 is lost for Black at (0,0): for every Black move (B14, A14, A13, B13, C15, D15, E19, pass), White connects at A19 and the result is DEAD, checked with two- and three-ply case checks against the solver's verdicts. The same holds when Black plays a lower-side move instead of answering B19 (W A18, B B17 forced, W A19 reaches the same positions). F19/G19 only add first-line outside liberties and cannot make a second eye. No double ko, 10kKO, bent four or seki is involved; the description is empty and the goal is only the group's life; the tree uses KO+2 elsewhere, so it does use threat-count labels. So the tree's KO- (s >= o+1) is wrong by one threat; the right label is KO-2. Sign '-' and class KO are unchanged, so the checker's class-and-sign comparison would not catch it; the error is only in the number. Scripts: /tmp/claude-0/proto/research/scratch/9-c001-definitions/ (probe.py, medium.py, andor.py).

checks.explanation:
I could not refute the claim: the tree's S[KO+] is wrong and the right label is KO-.

At the leaf, White's A18 is the first capture of the ko. It takes the lone stone on A19, and Black's A19 before it was only an atari on B19-C19, not a capture. Black's A17-B17-C17-B18 is in atari at C18, and Black cannot retake at A19 without a threat. I checked every other Black move by hand:
- C18 lets White capture eight stones at E19.
- E19 lets White capture both groups at C18.
- A pass lets White capture at C18, and D18-E18-D19 is left in atari and dead.

After a threat and the retake at A19, White cannot connect at C18 (suicide). If White plays E19 or passes, Black captures two stones at C18 and lives with eyes at A18 and B19/C19. So White needs its own threat to retake at A18. Neither side has a local threat. The area model is fine here: Black has no stones outside, and both White walls have plenty of outside liberties.

Counting threats, Black loses when the threats are equal and wins with one more than White. That is KO- ("White takes first"). The solver agrees in both areas. It also gives KO- at the two earlier nodes of this line (B18 C19 D19 B19 and the position after A19), so Black never gets to take first anywhere in this branch.

The author already labelled the identical A19-A18 ko in the C18 branch KO-, so no consistent convention gives KO+ here.

Side note: the solver finds the root ALIVE through C19. So the B18 line is a failing branch either way, and only this leaf's sign is wrong.

At the leaf, White's last move A18 is the first capture of the ko: Black's A19 before it was only an atari on B19-C19, so White took first. Black is to play under the ko ban, and its A17-B17-C17-B18 is in atari at C18. Every local Black move dies: C18 leaves only E19 and White E19 captures; after E19 or a pass, White C18 captures. So Black needs an outside threat to retake. After that retake (A19!), White C18 is suicide, and White E19 or a pass lets Black capture two at C18 and live with two eyes, so White needs a threat. This is a plain direct ko with no local threats and no approach moves: Black wins only with s >= o+1. That is besogo's KO- (extraThreats -1, "White takes first"), not KO+ ("Black takes first", s >= o), with no number and no approach prefix. Solver checks: leaf tables are no at s-o 0 and yes at +1, giving KO-; after A19! they are yes at 0, giving KO+, exactly one threat better. Before the leaf: A18 is White's only move; at the grandparent A19 is Black's only move that doesn't die; from B18 on, every node is KO-, so no Black alternative in this branch gives a ko Black takes first. The author marked the identical ko in the C18 branch (Black A19 atari, White A18 capture) KO-, and the solver agrees there, so KO+ is inconsistent under any single convention. Nothing in the description ("Black to live"), seki, bent four, ten-thousand-year ko or double ko changes this. A likely cause is besogo's editor, where choosing "ko" starts at KO+ (extraThreats 0) until the author presses "-".

analysis.summary: The tree is right: White lives by double ko. After White retakes at A13 there are two kos, A18/A19 at the top and A13/A14 at the bottom, and White needs only one of them. If Black settles the top with C19, White captures at A11 and connects out to the B10 stone. If Black protects with A11, White ataris at B11 and Black must recapture at A14. From then on, whenever Black retakes one ko, White takes the other without needing a threat, so Black can never settle both. The solver says DEAD only because its search area stops just below A12: A10 and B11 count as Black wall for it, so White's lower stones can never reach B10. (Context: Black's earlier B12, the KO+ sibling, is the move that avoids this.)

checks.explanation: I tried to refute S[ADKO] and could not; the tree is right and the solver's DEAD is an artifact of its search area. Apart from this corner, the SGF has only the lone White stone at B10 on an empty board, so once White captures A12 its stones connect to B10 and run into open space. Black has only one try at the leaf, A11. In model 1 (a living White group added under B10), every other Black move (C19, A18, B17, A16, B11, C12, A10 or pass) is met by White A11, which captures A12 and connects out: ALIVE. The decisive line is A11 B11 (atari) A14 (forced retake) A18. In that position every Black move except the banned retake at A19 gives ALIVE (A=N D=N for all). After A19! A13 the same holds: every Black move except the banned retake at A14 gives ALIVE (C19 lets White A10 capture and escape). So Black spends a threat on every retake while White always retakes the other ko for free, and the position repeats. Black cannot win with any number of threats. The counted search fails at s=1, and s=2 stays undecided even at a 2M budget, but the repetition settles it. White also has nothing better than this double ko after A11: no White reply in the model is clean life. C19, B11 and A10 give KO. A18 and A14 are undecided; A18 only reaches the same double ko, and filling at A14 lets Black B11 turn it into a single ko, which is worse for White. That matches the site's own definition of double ko ("if one ko is taken, the other can be taken by the other player"), so S[ADKO] is the right label. The solver says DEAD only because it treats A10, B11, C10 and B9 as Black wall, so in its model White can never escape through B10.

analysis.summary: The leaf is a ko that White takes first at B17, so KO- is the obvious label. But White also has a local ko threat at C18. After Black retakes at A17, White C18 puts the whole black group in atari at B17. Black has to capture the three stones at C19, and then White can retake at B17 again. The extra eye space does not settle it: Black still faces a ko where White took first. So Black has to win the ko twice and needs two more threats than White, which is KO-2 in besogo. The site's tutorial counts local ko threats in the sign, and its step-ko rule fits exactly: once Black has won the ko once, it becomes a plain KO-. The tree's KO- would mean one extra threat is enough, and that is false.

I read the position myself and agree with the analyst on the facts. At the leaf (Black to play), White's A17-A18-A19 have only B17 and B19 as liberties, and Black shares both. Black's outside liberties are D19, D16 and A15.
- **Black can't capture early.** If Black plays B19 or B17 and then captures, he gets a straight three, White places at A18, and Black is dead. The solver agrees (DEAD after B19 or B17).
- **So Black waits.** White fills A15, D16 and D19, answering Black D19 with E18 and later E19. Black is then left with only B17 and B19. Solver: B19/B17 DEAD, pass BENT4 (9 s).
- **White makes the bent four.** White sacrifices at B19 and Black must capture four stones with B17. That leaves A17-A18-A19-B19, a bent four with the bend on the corner point A19. White plays A18. Black's only move is A19 (A17, B19 and pass are DEAD). White B19 captures, and Black's whole group is in atari at A17. Solver: KO+ in both the search area and the wider area (6 s).
- **Black can never start this ko; only White can, at a moment it chooses.** If White sacrifices before filling the outside liberties, Black lives with A17 and then A19. If White sacrifices at B17 instead, Black gets a living L-shaped four. White fills first, which it always can.
- **The site's own rules call this dead.** It is the same kind of seki-looking shape as the site tutorial's bent-four example (/img/d-bentfour.png), which the tutorial calls dead under the site's Japanese rules. It is exactly what besogo's BENT4 status describes, and the author's comment on this leaf says bent four.

What's left, DEAD or BENT4, is the labelling question the brief lists under definitions. The analyst's question leaves out the effect on grading, explained in the correction.

I could not refute the analyst. At the leaf White has just taken the ko at B19. Black's group has two liberties, B17 and A15, and no local threat: White's wall from D18 round to B15 has 9 liberties, and Black's moves at A15, A14, B14 or A13 only give White time to fill A19.

**With no threats on either side, Black dies.** Black passes or plays a waiting move, White fills at A19, and Black takes four stones at B17. White plays A18 at once, Black A19, and White takes this second ko first at B19. Black still has no threat, so White fills, Black A17 takes three, and White A19 kills the bent three.

**With one more threat than White, Black lives.** Black retakes A19, and White cannot save A17-A18 because B17 is suicide for White. So Black wins only when s >= o+1, which is KO-.

**The one real hole I found is outside liberties, and it doesn't work.** If Black has two outside liberties when it takes the four stones, the bent four lives: after A18, A19, B19, Black plays A17 and both White stones are left with A19 as their only liberty. The solver confirms this: after A15 A19 A14 pass B17 A18 it gives ALIVE in the wider area. But White can always hold Black to one outside liberty:
- Black A15, then White A19 (forced, or Black retakes for free).
- Black A14 now has two liberties, but White blocks at B14.
- Black A13 gets only A12, because of White's B13 stone, and White A12 makes Black take the four stones with none left.
- The lines through B14 or C14, and Black's tries that start with A13 or B14, are stopped the same way. So this also holds on the real, open board, not just inside the solver's area.

**Solver checks:**
- Leaf + pass A19, and leaf + A15, A14, B14 or A13 followed by White A19: Black fails at s-o=0 and wins at +1, in both areas.
- In the bent four after White A18, only Black A19 keeps the ko; A17, A15, B19 and pass are DEAD.

**Why the tree says KO+:** selecting "ko" in besogo's editor starts the threat counter at 0, which is saved as KO+. The author also labels every ko in the L Group series KO+. But by besogo's own definition (KO+ means "Black takes first") and the site tutorial's KO- diagram, where the opponent has just captured, this leaf is KO-.

The analyst is right: the leaf should be KO-, not KO+. White's last move, B19, captured Black's A19 stone in a one-stone ko, so Black is to play but cannot retake yet. Black's group has two liberties (B17, A15); White's A17-A18 has two (A19, B17).
- **Black has one more threat:** Black uses it, retakes at A19, and A17-A18 are in atari. White has no threat left, so Black captures at B17 and is ALIVE.
- **Threats are equal:** Black runs out first. White fills A19 and Black captures four at B17. White must play A18 at once (otherwise Black A18 lives), Black must play A19, and White must take at B19 (otherwise Black A17 lives). White has taken this second ko first as well, so Black needs a threat again and dies.
So Black lives only when s >= o+1. In besogo that is extraThreats -1, which status.js names 'White takes first', i.e. KO-.

The tutorial says KO+ still fits when White took first but Black has a local threat. There is none here:
- B17 is self-atari; White captures the group at A15.
- A15, A14, B14 and A13 are all answered by the fill at A19. White keeps Black at one outside liberty, so the A17 trick inside the second ko never works.
- In both search areas, pass, A15, A14, B14 and A13 followed by White A19 give no at s-o=0 and yes at +1, and B17 is DEAD. That closes the wider area's '?' at the leaf.

The details of KO- also hold. White has no local threat (the solver gives yes at s=1, o=0), so it is not KO-2. No approach moves are needed. The two kos do not add up to a step ko, because White takes first in both. Neither ko gives a seki.

The description asks only that the target lives. The comment on the sibling SEKI+ line calls the ko too dangerous, which fits KO-.

The sign was probably never chosen. In the besogo editor a plain 'Ko' button gives extraThreats 0, which displays as KO+, and the whole L Group series never uses KO-. That explains the slip but is not a convention the definitions allow.

One small correction to the analyst: the bent four here is not 'dead outright'. White has to start that ko at once, so it is an ordinary ko where White takes first. The label is KO- either way.

Besogo uses the same meaning. better() puts KO+ above KO- for the first player whatever the goal, and transformTextColors turns 'Black takes first' into 'White takes first' when White plays first. The editor's status label is not turned the same way, which probably misled the author. The author's own sibling problem 15298 labels a leaf where Black took first in a White-first problem S[KO-], with the comment 'your opponent takes first'. In the whole corpus of White-first problems, 24 leaves where White took last are KO+ and 5 where Black took last are KO-. So S[KO+] here is wrong; it should be KO-.

The tree's KO+ is wrong and KO- is the right label. At the leaf, Black's A18 has just captured White's A17, so the opponent took the ko first, and White (the solver) is to play. White can't retake at once. B16 and B19 are suicide for White, and E18 threatens nothing, so White has no local threat. If White passes or plays elsewhere, Black B19 (or A17) lives. If White retakes A17 after a threat, Black's B16, B19 and pass all lose to W B16 then B19, so Black must find a threat of his own. Black's only possible local threat in the corner is E18 or F19 against E19, and it doesn't count. After W A17!, B E18, White can ignore it with B16, taking three stones. Black F19 then captures E19, but W E17 or G19 still kills: E19 is a false eye, and any new ko at E19 leaves Black eyeless even if he wins it. Even if it counted, it could only push the label further minus, never to plus.

Besogo's definitions are from the solver's side:
- Its ranking (`better()`) prefers a higher threat count for the solver whatever the goal.
- The message players see swaps the colour words in White-first problems, so KO+ reads "White takes first".
- The site tutorial's KO- picture is the case where the opponent just captured.

The only colour-based text is the editor's status label. It doesn't swap colours, so here it shows "KO+ (Black takes first)", which is the likely cause of the error but doesn't make KO+ correct. - H19 is White's best answer. A19 instead gives Black more local threats with the throw-in at B18 or B19.
- E18 is a free retake, and the position is exactly the sibling leaf the tree labels KO+. I checked that the boards are the same, and the solver also says KO+.

I re-ran the counted searches in the wider area:
- At the leaf with s=0, o=1, Black wins after every White move (A19 A17 D19 E17! H19 J19 K19 pass).
- After E17! A17, Black wins against every White reply, both at s=0, o=0 and at s=1, o=1. So the leaf with s=1, o=2 is also a Black win.
- With two extra threats White wins. After E17! A17 H19 E18 E17! at s=0, o=0, Black fails after every move. A19 is answered by A18, which captures three stones and lives in the corner. J19 is answered by E18. Black's other replies to the first E17! also fail.

These White wins don't depend on the solver's G19-ko artifact, which only appears when White still has two or more threats. So Black wins exactly when s >= o-1. That is besogo's KO+2 (extraThreats=1, "White needs 1 threat to start the ko"), with + for the sign, 2 for the number and no approach moves.

It is not an approach ko, because White can retake at once and the ko is direct. It is not a double ko or a ten-thousand-year ko, because White can never win the G19 ko. The tutorial says local ko threats are counted. Its step-ko wording also fits: White winning the ko once doesn't settle the status, and it then becomes the KO+ sibling. The tree gives this leaf and its sibling the same KO+, although they differ by exactly Black's free A17 threat.

The practical impact is small: either label is a ko, which is worse than the DEAD main line, so only the S[] precision changes.

analysis.summary: At the leaf Black has just taken the ko at A19, so White needs a ko threat to retake at A18. Winning that ko does not kill Black, though. So White must win a second, direct ko in which Black has again taken first. White therefore needs one more threat than in a plain KO+. With one White threat against none for Black, Black still lives. This is the site's own 'step ko' (KO+2, which becomes KO+ once the opponent has won it once), so the leaf should be S[KO+2], not S[KO+]. The leaf sits in a wrong-answer branch (the correct first moves give SEKI), so the fix changes only the status shown for this branch, not which moves count as correct.

checks.explanation: I could not refute the analyst. The tree's S[KO+] is too low for Black, and the correct status is KO+2. At the leaf, Black has just taken the ko at A19, and White's only resource is to retake A18 with a threat. Every other White move fails: C19 lets Black capture three stones at D18, D18 lets Black capture three at C19, and if White plays elsewhere Black lives with C19. After the retake, Black has no local threat: C19 and D18 are both self-ataris, and White captures the whole group at D18 or C19. Even with no threats, though, Black is not dead. White cannot finish the ko. Filling at A19 is self-atari (Black C19 takes three). D18 lets Black take two stones at C19, then two more at A19, and Black has two eyes. So White has to atari at C19, and Black retakes A19 immediately without a threat, which puts B19-C19-C18 in atari. That starts a second direct ko that Black has again taken first; D18 is now illegal for White (suicide). So White must win two kos that Black took first, and Black lives whenever s >= o-1. Concretely: one White threat against none, Black lives; two against none, White kills; two against one, Black lives; three against one, White kills. That is exactly KO+2, and it matches the site tutorial's step ko ('KO+2 becomes KO+ once the opponent has won it once'): the position after White's first ko win is a plain KO+. I checked this three ways. The solver gives the leaf tables (-1 yes, -2 no), shows the position after White's first win as KO+, and shows the position after C19 and the free A19 retake as KO+. An independent brute-force search on the real 19x19 board gives the same results. Neither side has a local threat at any point. The site also uses KO+2 elsewhere for a leaf that ends with the solver capturing a ko (problem 9820), so KO+ here is an oversight, not a convention. My scripts and outputs are in /tmp/claude-0/proto/research/scratch/10974-c048-reading/ (brute.py, brute_out.txt, lines.py, leaf_lines.txt, p2_moves.txt, p3_ko.txt).

The tree's S[KO+] is wrong, but the exact label is A+1KO+, not KO+2. The two mean the same in ko-threat counts.

Why KO+ is wrong: at the leaf, Black has just taken at A19 and White is to play. Every White move other than retaking at A18 (C19, D18, pass) lets Black live. White's retake at A18 needs a threat, and it is not an atari: Black's group still has C19 and D18. Black can therefore ignore it. White must then fill C19, and Black retakes A19 without a threat. I confirmed this with the solver: after A18! pass C19, Black's only good move is A19, which keeps a plain KO+, while a pass gives DEAD. White has to win the ko a second time, so White needs two more threats than Black. The ko tables show Black lives at s-o=-1 and dies at -2 in both areas. With s=0 and o=1, Black lives, which a plain KO+ would score as dead. Neither side has a local threat. It is not a 10kKO, since the ko is already being fought and Black lives if White stops. It is not a double ko either.

Why A+1KO+ rather than KO+2: the extra step is an approach move. White's capture is not atari until White fills the liberty at C19, and that fill gives Black a free retake. That is a one-move approach ko where Black took first. Besogo's own wording for A+1KO+ describes it exactly: "White needs to do 1 approach move to start a direct ko, Black takes first."

The site already uses this label for the same position. Problem 2521 (Intermediate 489), line B18 C18 D19 A18 A19, reaches the identical stones, ko point and side to play, and it is marked S[A+1KO+]. I ran the solver there and got the same KO+2 table. The site also gives A+1KO+ to the same kind of shape in problem 2406, where White's retake leaves Black with two liberties and White has to fill F19.

KO+2 is the counted-threat equivalent. Its sign (+) and number (2) are right, it fits the tutorial's step-ko description, and the checker would accept it. But it counts the approach move as an extra threat, and it would contradict 2521.

The B18 branch is wrong either way, because the correct first moves give SEKI. So the fix only changes the status this branch shows, not which moves count as correct.

analysis.summary: This leaf is a ko, not dead. If Black wins the corner ko (retake at A19, later connect at A18), it lives. The solver says DEAD only because its small search area treats A12/B12 as White's wall, so White's crawl down the edge kills even when Black wins every ko. But KO-2 undercounts White's local threats. The author only counted the B14/A15 exchange from the sibling KO- line. White does better with the placement at A15 (Black must answer B14) and then pushes down the first line: A14 (B13), A13 (A12), B12 (Black captures at A16) and A14 again. Each of these lets White retake the ko without an outside threat, so Black needs about six more threats than White: KO-6 in the solver's wider area. Black needs at least three more in any reading, which already rules out KO-2; on a fully open board the count may be one lower (KO-5).

The tree's KO-2 can't be defended, but KO-6 isn't proven either. The sign and the ko type are right: White just retook at A18, so White took first, and the ko is direct with no approach moves. The author counted only one local White threat, B14, the exchange in the sibling KO- line. White does better: after Black retakes at A19, the placement W A15 (Black's only answer is B14), then W A14 (only answer B13), then W A13 (answer A12 or B12). Each of these kills if Black connects the ko instead. I read that on an open board, and the solver confirms it in the 2- and 3-ring areas. judges.explanation:
At the leaf, White has just retaken at A18, and B18-C18-C17 is in atari. Black must win the ko: saving the stones at B17 dies in every frame. The tree's KO-2 counts one free White threat, the B14/A15 exchange from the sibling KO- line. White has better. After Black retakes, White places at A15. If Black connects the ko instead of answering, White B14 (joined to C14) seals the corner and kills, so Black has to answer B14. Then White A14 forces B13 the same way (White B13, joined to C13, kills). Both are free retakes in any frame, so KO-2 is too low however the edge is closed.

What comes next depends on how much room the empty edge below C13 gives Black, and the SGF does not say (no stones there). I closed the edge with explicit White stones and checked each frame with the solver:
- Edge closed at row 11 or nearer (W A11 B11 C11 C12, W A12 B12 C12, or W A13 B13): after the retake, White A15 kills outright, even if Black may ignore the ko ban. The leaf is DEAD. The solver's own search area treats A13/B13 as White's wall, which is why it says DEAD.
- Edge closed at row 10 (W A10 B10 C10 C11 C12): White has five free threats: A15/B14, A14/B13, A13/A12, B12/A16, A14/A13. After them, a White pass lets Black connect and live, so the leaf is KO-6. This matches the analyst's KO-6 in the solver's wider area.
- More room: Black answers better (B12 instead of A12 to White's A13 with the edge closed at row 9), so the count drops, to about KO-5 there and roughly KO-4 on a fully open edge. With a lot of room, Black might even live along the side by giving up the corner stones; the solver could not settle that.

The tree's main line needs the room. Its position after B18 A18 A17 B19 B15 C19 A19 is this leaf after Black's retake, and in the tighter frames White A15 kills there as well. So the label that fits the rest of the tree is a minus ko with about five White threats, not KO-2. There are four small corrections, and none of them changes the verdict.

After Black G19 and a capture at E19, White's D19 group is in atari, and every White move except the retake is plain DEAD. That is dead for the same reason (Black removes the threats first), but it is not a corner bent four. BENT4 ranks above DEAD for White, so White's best defence is to connect at C18 and accept the corner bent four. BENT4 is therefore still the exact label.
(3) The claim that "+pass G19 gives BENT4/DEAD for every White reply" is not fully confirmed by the solver. At 200k nodes, White's pass and the outside replies (C15, D15, E15, F15) stay undecided. The pass is case (2). The outside moves only attack Black's outer stones, which look short of liberties only because the search area is narrow.

At the leaf White is to play. White's A16-B18 group has liberties A17 and C18, its D19-E17 group has C18 and E16, and Black's E19 stone is in atari.

White A17 lets Black C18 capture six stones (DEAD). Every other White try ends in the same corner. After C18 F19, after pass F19 (where every White move except C18 is plain DEAD), or after F19 E16 (the c067 position) followed by C18, White's groups are joined at C18. White captures two stones at A19, Black takes back at B19, Black later fills E16, and the E19 point gets settled. Connecting at E19 gains White nothing once Black has G19.

What remains is the classic seki-looking bent four in the corner:
- White's one group has only the liberties A17 and C19, shared with Black A18 and B19.
- White B18 sits on the 2-2 point, and the corner point A19 is empty.
- White has no move there: A17 and C19 are self-atari, and A19 is illegal.

Whenever it likes, Black can play A19 and A17; White C19 captures four stones; then A18, A19, B19. Black has taken the ko first and White is in atari at A17. A White A17 attack while White still has a spare liberty fails to Black A19, and the solver gives DEAD for it.

Solver results on that shape:
- Plain search: KO.
- Search with no ko captures allowed: A=N D=N, so the result is not plain DEAD. The leaf itself gives the same.
- Counted threats: Black wins at s-o=0 and loses at -1, which is KO+.
- Bent-four rule: Black kills in 117 nodes.

At the leaf itself the bent-four search is still undecided at 200k nodes, so the tool falls back to KO+. That is the counted-threat result for this same ko, in which ko threats can never be removed.

So the real question is the label: DEAD (the site's Japanese rule that bent four in the corner is dead) or BENT4 (besogo's exact label). Neither the tree nor the solver is simply wrong.

It is a direct ko with no approach moves, not a step ko. With equal threats: pass, A18, B17, pass, A16, A18 gives DEAD. With one more threat for Black: A18!, pass, B17 gives ALIVE. The solver's ko tables (0 no, +1 yes) give the same answer. No bent four, seki, 10kKO or double ko is involved, and the goal ("live unconditionally") asks for nothing beyond the group's life. The position after C19, with White to play: White's group has four liberties (A16, B18, D18, F19). Black's B19-C19-D19 has three (A19, B18, D18), and A18 has two (A19, B18).

- Who took first: C19 captured nothing, and White does take first after B18.
- The extra point is a real tempo: Black needs one more threat than in a direct ko.

KO-2 matches the site's own tutorial definition: once Black wins the ko once, it becomes KO-. The same position in approach-ko notation is A-1KO- (Black needs one approach move at A16, White takes first). That also means s >= o + 2, and besogo's ordering ranks it a little lower than KO-2. One move's mark changes: Black's 5th move B18 (after D17 D19 E19 B19) goes from correct to wrong. The problem's own status also changes, from 10kKO to ALIVE. Both changes are wrong.

The c016 fix is right on its own: after White's C18 mistake, Black lives. But C18 is White's only reply to A17 in the tree. So besogo concludes that A17 lives outright, makes it the only best move, and calls the whole problem ALIVE. White has stronger replies to A17 that the tree leaves out:

B17, C17 and C19 are self-ataris, and A18 and B19 are illegal. Black's only possible local threat is E19, the atari on D19, and it fails: E19 C19 (takes B19), B19 (takes C19 and D19), C19 (takes B19), D19, B19. The white corner then keeps the shared liberties A18 and B17. Black can't fill them, because it would first have to play C17 and B17 and would need two outside liberties. The solver agrees: Black is DEAD after E19, and after E19 C19 B19 C19, in both modes in the search area, with every Black alternative dead. After Black retakes (A18!), every White move except the retake (B17, C17, C19, E19, F19, pass) lets Black live with B17, which captures B18, A17 and A16 (solver ALIVE for all). White has taken first, and Black cannot play A17 because that is self-atari. My run: KO, sign KO+ in both areas, and every Black move other than a retake is DEAD.

That is the textbook bent four in the corner. It is dead under the problem's RU[Japanese] rules. Otherwise it is a ko that White can start whenever it likes. Besogo's exact label for it is BENT4, ranked just above DEAD. The author's comment shows the DEAD label was a deliberate choice.

facts.correction:
The position and lines are right, but three points need adding or fixing.
(1) The tutorial does not say what the analyst quotes. Its sentence is "small sacrifices are a failure most of the time". Giving up the five top stones (four of White's ten original stones) is not a small sacrifice, so the tutorial does not settle this case.
(2) This leaf is not a one-off mistake at G19. The tree's main line (its first variation, case c120) ends the same way and is also S[DEAD]: White takes B15 with a single stone at A15, plays B17, and lives with eyes at A16 and B15, while only the top stones die. Across the whole tree, every DEAD leaf kills the top stones. Every ALIVE leaf is a line where the top stones survive by capturing Black's cutting stones. The SEKI leaves leave the top stones alive in seki. So the tree consistently scores the top stones.
(3) The "whole group" option is weaker than it sounds. "A15 there is the tree's kill" holds only if the lower side is closed. The SGF has no stones below row 13, so B13-B14-C13 can always run out to the open lower side. The wall goes with them, because a throw-in at A15 or B15 connects the two chains. On the board as given, even the A15 lines kill only the top stones, and no line in the tree kills the whole group. At the leaf (White to play), the top chain D19-D18-E18-F18-G18 has one liberty, E19. White E19 is suicide. White's B19 or A19 against Black's corner (A18-B18-C18-C19, liberties A19 and B19) is one move too slow, because Black simply captures at E19. So those five stones die. With the target set to D18-G18 only, the solver kills in both areas and both modes.

The rest of White lives. A17-B17-C17-C16-C15-B16 has two eyes at A16 and B15. Black can never fill either eye: both moves are suicide. For the same reason Black can never capture A15. B13-B14-C13 stays joined to the rest through A13/A14, which are miai: if Black plays A14, White captures it with A13; if Black plays A13, White connects at A14.

The solver confirms ALIVE for the whole group at the leaf, and even after White passes twice: after "pass E19 pass", every one of Black's 16 moves still leaves White alive.

So DEAD is right for the top stones and ALIVE for the whole group. The SGF names no target and has no description, so neither side is wrong under besogo's definitions; which stones the problem is about is the owner's call. The evidence leans towards the top stones: the tree scores them consistently, including in its main line, and the whole group cannot be killed on the open board. That reading means keeping DEAD and stating the goal in the description.

facts.correction:
The analyst is right about the leaf itself. Two of the supporting claims are wrong, and both concern the "whole group" option given to the owner.
(1) "The solver agrees DEAD at its leaf" for the sibling (B15 B16 A18 D19 E17 C19 G19 B19 F19 A17 A15 A14 H19 A16 E19) is not reproduced. I get "?" in both areas and both modes at 200k and at 1M nodes, and "?" after every White move. The checker's own run also had "?" there.
(2) "If the whole group, move the main line to Black's A15 at move 11" is not a fix that works. In the sibling, A15 and B15 are miai, so the C15-C17 chain stays joined to B13-B14-C13. Those stones face open board: there is no Black stone below row 14. The sibling's "two-point eye" kill exists only because the solver treats its region edge as a Black wall, and even inside that model the solver cannot prove it. With the lower side open, no DEAD leaf in the tree kills the left side. So choosing the whole group as the goal would leave the problem with no correct answer; it would not just move the main line.
Minor: "lives without conditions" is fair (no ko and no threats are needed), but White must answer Black's A14 with A13, or A13 with A14 (they are miai).
facts.explanation:
At the leaf (White to play), the seven top stones B19-C19-D19-D18-E18-F18-G18 have one liberty, A19. White cannot fill it: A19 is suicide while A18-B18-C18 still has B17. So the top stones are lost.

White B17 is sente because it puts A18-B18-C18 in atari. Black must take the seven stones at A19. White's left side then keeps two real eyes, A16 and B15, and Black can never play either point. After B17 A19 A14 the left side is unconditionally alive. If Black throws in at A14 instead, A13 captures it.

The other orders change nothing. If White passes, Black's capture at A19 is gote and White plays B17 next. If Black plays B17 before capturing, it is self-atari, and White takes four stones at A19.

The solver agrees with this reading. For the whole group it gives ALIVE in both areas and both modes. With the target set to D18-G18 only, it gives DEAD in both.

So the S[] depends only on which stones count as the target, and neither side misreads the position. The problem has only G[KILL] and no description that names the stones, so it is a question about the goal.

The facts strongly favour the top stones as the target:
- B13-B14-C13 face open board.
- The C15-C17 side stays joined to them, or has two eyes, in every DEAD leaf of the tree.
- The main line itself kills only the top.

In practice the owner should keep DEAD and state the goal, for example "capture the top stones". My scripts and survey are in /tmp/claude-0/proto/research/scratch/15678-c120-facts/.

checks.explanation:
I could not refute it: S[KO+] is wrong under every reading of the target. The right label depends on the target. It is ALIVE for the whole White group, which is the solver's target and the analyst's answer. It is KO-2 for the top stones only, which is what this tree scores everywhere else. I recommend KO-2.

Why KO+ cannot be right: at the leaf White has just captured at A18. Black is banned from A17, and the four corner stones (A19, B18, C18, C19) are in atari at B19. B19 is suicide for Black. Black has no local threat, because White answers any local move with B19, capturing four stones and joining everything. So with equal threats, even s=o=0, Black fails. The site tutorial calls exactly this case KO- or worse.

Whole group: after A17! (a ko threat, then the retake), White plays B15 and the left stones join B14 and run out to the open lower side. The solver finds no kill even when Black may ignore the ko ban (mode D), in both areas. So the group is ALIVE, as the analyst says.

Top stones only: this is the target the tree uses. Its DEAD main line (c119/c120) leaves the left side free to escape at B15, and its A-2KO+ and SEKI leaves come after White has already connected at B15. On this reading, Black must win the ko twice. In the line A17! B15 E17 A18, White retakes for free and Black needs a second threat. The solver agrees: from that position, Black wins with one threat more than White and fails with equal threats, in both areas.

White's H19 does not add a threat:
- While the top stones have three liberties, Black answers H19 with B15. After that, every Black retake puts the left stones in atari, and if White takes G19 with F19, Black B16 captures four stones and wins the race.
- At two liberties H19 fails at once: Black F19, then a snapback at G19. The solver confirms Black kills in both modes.

So the top stones are KO-2: Black fails with one extra threat and wins with two. That matches the analyst's own count, not the KO-3 I first got on a simplified board, which had removed Black's B15 answer.

My scripts are in /tmp/claude-0/proto/research/scratch/15678-c121-reading/ (topcount.py, toponly.py, show.py).

KO+ is wrong however the target is read, but ALIVE is not settled as the right label either.

Why KO+ is wrong: White's A18 was the ko capture, so White took first. Black has no local threat, because any Black move except the retake lets White take four stones at B19. Black also can never close the ko, because A18 and B19 are both self-atari. Under besogo's rules that rules out KO+.

ALIVE is right only for the solver's whole-group target. That target counts White as alive if any part lives, and after A17! B15 the left side has eyes at B16 and A15. The tree's own main line shows the real target is the top four stones, D18-G18: its DEAD leaves (c119, c120) kill only those stones while the left side lives. For those stones the leaf is a ko where White took first.
- Black must retake with a threat. After White's B15 (or a pass), Black fills one of the three liberties (E17, E19, F19). White then retakes for free and Black has to win the ko again. That means Black needs two more threats than White (s >= o+2), which is KO-2 by the plain count. The analyst got this too.
- By my reading it is KO-3. With three liberties left, White's H19 atari on G19 is a free local threat. If Black answers J19, White retakes for free. If Black counters with B15, it becomes a ko for the B17-C15 chain, where White still has a free E17 threat to escape through E16 and connect to C13.

The solver could not settle the number. With only the top stones as target, every ko count was undecided. One check held: after A17! B15, Black wins with one more threat than White, which fits the count. The search area also treats E16 as a wall, so it cannot see the E17 escape.

So the right S[] depends on the same target question as c119/c120, and for the problem's real target it is KO-2 or KO-3, not ALIVE. My scripts are in /tmp/claude-0/proto/research/scratch/15678-c121-definitions/ (top.py, show.py).

judges.explanation:
S[KO+] is wrong whatever the target. White's A18 was the ko capture, so White took first. Black's A19 and B18-C18-C19 hang at B19, and A18 and B19 are both self-atari for Black. Black has no local threat either: any move except the retake lets White take four stones at B19 and join everything.

Whole White group (the solver's target): after Black's A17! retake, White connects at B15 and the left side lives. The solver finds no kill even when Black may ignore the ko ban, so this reading gives ALIVE, as the analyst said.

Top stones D18-G18 only (what the tree's DEAD main line scores, see c119/c120): Black has to hold the ko while it fills E17, F19 and E19, and White retakes for free after each fill. On its own that is KO-2. But White also has H19, an atari on G19. If Black takes it at J19, White retakes for free. If Black counters with B15, White retakes, and Black's next retake puts B17-C15 in atari. White then pushes at E17, threatening to escape through E16. Black must block at E16, and White retakes for free again. So Black needs three more threats than White: KO-3. Reviewer 1's KO-2 missed the E17 push, because the solver's narrow area treats E16, which is empty on the real board, as a Black wall. Reviewer 2's KO-3 is right.

Checked with the engine on a hand-built board. The B14 group is made unconditionally alive, E16 opens onto an alive White group, J19, K19 and J18 are playable, and the target is D18-G18. The losing results with 2 threats were also played out by hand, since only the winning results are guaranteed sound for this engine.
